label: Timing-driven routing
prereqs: Elmore delay of an RC tree
lesson:
# Timing-driven routing

A timing-driven router blends delay and congestion in each node's cost, weighted by how critical the connection is. Critical connections pay mostly for delay and take fast routes even if congested; non-critical ones pay mostly for congestion and detour. VPR's router uses this cost with criticalities refreshed by static timing analysis between iterations.

## Criticality

After a timing analysis, the router assigns each source-sink connection $\mathrm{Crit}(i,j) = \max\left(0, \mathrm{MaxCrit} - \mathrm{slack}(i,j)/D_{max}\right)$, with $\mathrm{MaxCrit}$ just below 1, for example 0.99. A connection on the critical path gets 0.99, not 1, so a little congestion pressure always remains and even the most critical net can be pushed off an overused wire. With $D_{max} = 2850$ ps and slack 810 ps, $\mathrm{Crit} = 0.99 - 0.284 = 0.706$. VPR can also raise criticality to an exponent to sharpen the distinction. Criticalities are updated once per iteration from the current routing, so they follow the router as delays change.

## The node cost

The timing-driven cost of node $n$ for connection $(i, j)$ is $\mathrm{Crit}(i,j) \cdot \mathrm{delay}(n) + (1 - \mathrm{Crit}(i,j)) \cdot b(n) h(n) p(n)$, with delays normalized to the scale of the congestion term. With $\mathrm{Crit} = 0.9624$, a node delay of 2.25, $b = 1$, $h = 3$ and $p = 1$, the cost is $0.9624 \times 2.25 + 0.0376 \times 3 = 2.278$. The delay term is the Elmore delay the node adds to the partial route, which depends on the upstream resistance of the tree being built. The congestion term is PathFinder's, with history applied multiplicatively in VPR's form. Because both are priced in the same search, one wavefront handles both objectives.

## Choosing between fast and free paths

Given two paths, the router compares $\mathrm{Crit} \cdot \mathrm{delay} + (1 - \mathrm{Crit}) \cdot \mathrm{congestion}$ for each. A connection with slack 1230 ps out of $D_{max} = 1980$ ps has $\mathrm{Crit} = 0.369$. Path 1, delay 5 and congestion 19, costs $0.369 \times 5 + 0.631 \times 19 = 13.84$; path 2, delay 13 and congestion 5, costs 7.95, so the connection detours on path 2 and frees path 1 for critical nets. The effect over many nets is that slack is spent where it exists. The risk is instability: as routes change, criticalities change, and a connection can flip between paths, which is why criticalities are refreshed per iteration rather than per net.

## Going deeper

Betz, Rose and Marquardt (1999), chapter 6; Swartz, Betz and Rose, FPGA (1998); the VPR router documentation for max_criticality and criticality_exp.

label: Minimum channel width search
lesson:
# Minimum channel width search

The minimum channel width $W_{min}$ is the smallest number of tracks per channel at which a circuit routes on a given architecture. It is the standard measure of routability in FPGA research: architectures and routers are compared by $W_{min}$ and by delay at a relaxed width. Finding it means routing many times, so the search procedure matters.

## Lower bounds from channel density

Before detailed routing, each channel's demand gives a lower bound. In a channel, nets crossing the same column need different tracks, so the channel needs at least its density: the maximum number of nets crossing any one column. With nets spanning columns 4 to 7, 6 to 9, 5 to 10 and 7 to 9, column 7 is crossed by all four, so that channel needs 4 tracks. $W$ must cover the densest channel, so $W_{min}$ is at least the maximum density over all channels. A real router may need more, because switch-box patterns and connection-box flexibility limit which tracks a net can switch between, as with the track domains of disjoint switch boxes.

## Searching for the minimum

VPR finds $W_{min}$ by routing repeatedly. Start at some width; while routing fails, double $W$; once a width succeeds, binary-search between the last failing and the first succeeding width, routing at the midpoint each time, until they differ by 1. If routing succeeds exactly when $W \ge 28$ and the search starts at $W = 2$, it tries 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 (five attempts), then 24, 28, 26 and 27 (four more), nine routings in all. Each attempt is a complete PathFinder run, and failing attempts are the slowest because they run to the iteration limit. Routability is assumed monotone in $W$, which holds in practice, though the router's heuristics can make it noisy near the threshold.

## Low-stress routing

Routing at exactly $W_{min}$ stresses the router: nets take long detours and the critical path grows. Architecture studies therefore report delay at a relaxed width, commonly $1.3 \, W_{min}$, which models a device with some routing headroom. Unidirectional architectures add a parity rule, because wires come in pairs driven in opposite directions, so $W$ must be even. With $W_{min} = 66$, $1.3 \times 66 = 85.8$ rounds up to 86, which is already even. A paper that reports a lower $W_{min}$ without delay at a low-stress width hides a possible trade: a router can buy routability with delay. Both numbers, together with run time, are needed to judge a change.

## Going deeper

Betz, Rose and Marquardt (1999), chapters 6 and 7; Rose et al., "The VTR Project: Architecture and CAD for FPGAs from Verilog to Routing", FPGA (2012).

lesson:
# FPGA timing analysis

FPGA timing analysis runs ordinary static timing on a graph whose delays come from the device: LUT and flip-flop delays from the timing database, routing delays from the routed path or, before routing, from a placement delay model indexed by distance. Placement, routing and the final report all use the same propagation; what changes is how good the routing delays are.

## Path arrival from a delay model

Before routing, VPR estimates the delay of a connection from a table indexed by $(|\Delta x|, |\Delta y|)$, built by routing sample connections through an empty fabric. A register-to-register path's arrival at the capture flip-flop is the clock-to-q delay, plus every LUT delay, plus the table delay of every connection. For a path launch FF at $(5, 3)$, LUT1 at $(7, 5)$, LUT2 at $(4, 5)$, capture FF at $(3, 5)$, the connections have offsets $(2, 2)$, $(3, 0)$ and $(1, 0)$. If those table entries are 290, 220 and 120 ps, with clock-to-q 50 ps and LUTs of 170 ps, the arrival is $50 + 290 + 170 + 220 + 170 + 120 = 1020$ ps. The table ignores congestion, so it is optimistic.

## Setup slack

With an ideal clock of period $T$, setup slack is $T - t_{su} - \mathrm{arrival}$. A path with arrival 1180 ps, setup 100 ps and $T = 1470$ ps has slack $1470 - 100 - 1180 = 190$ ps. A negative slack means the path fails at this clock. In a full analysis the clock arrives with skew at each flip-flop, and its network has its own routed delay; FPGA clock networks are dedicated, balanced trees, so skew is small but not zero, and vendors' timing reports include clock-path delays and uncertainty. The same arrival-required arithmetic from static timing analysis applies unchanged; only the source of each delay is FPGA-specific.

## Maximum frequency

If a path is critical, the shortest legal period is its arrival plus setup, and the maximum frequency is the reciprocal: $F_{max} = 10^6 / (\mathrm{arrival} + t_{su})$ MHz with delays in ps. For arrival 1310 ps and setup 60 ps, $F_{max} = 10^6 / 1370 = 729.9$ MHz. Because placement-stage delays omit congestion and detours, the post-route $F_{max}$ is usually lower; the gap is why placers recompute criticalities from estimates and routers recompute them from real routes. Open flows report $F_{max}$ from nextpnr's or VPR's own timer, vendor flows from their signoff timers, and the two use different delay data, so cross-tool comparisons need one timer applied to both results.

## Going deeper

Marquardt, Betz and Rose, FPGA (2000), for the placement delay model; Murray et al., "Tatum: Parallel Timing Analysis for Faster Design Cycles and Improved Optimization", FPT (2018).

label: Configuration bits and bitstreams
lesson:
# Configuration bits and bitstreams

The bitstream is the file that configures an FPGA: every LUT bit, every multiplexer select, every routing switch and every hard-block mode, organized into frames that the configuration logic writes. Bitstream generation is the last step of the flow and the only one whose output the hardware sees, so its size, structure and load time are part of the architecture.

## Counting configuration bits

Each tile contributes the bits of its logic and its routing. A tile with one cluster of $N$ BLEs of $k$-LUTs holds $N(2^k + 1)$ logic bits, and its share of connection and switch boxes adds one bit per switch. With $N = 8$, $k = 5$ and 910 routing bits, a tile holds $8 \times 33 + 910 = 1174$ bits, and a $35 \times 35$ array holds $1225 \times 1174 = 1{,}438{,}150$ bits, before I/O, clocking and hard blocks. Routing bits usually outnumber logic bits several times, which mirrors the area split: most of an FPGA is programmable interconnect. The bitstream is therefore mostly routing, and most of it is zeros for a lightly used device.

## Frames and load time

Configuration memory is written in frames, the smallest addressable unit, each a fixed number of bits that usually spans a column of tiles. A full configuration of $B$ bits in frames of $f$ bits needs $\lceil B/f \rceil$ frames. Load time is set by the configuration port: $B$ bits over a $w$-bit port at clock $F$ take $B / (wF)$ seconds. A 29-megabit device loaded over a 32-bit port at 100 MHz takes about 9 ms; over a 1-bit serial interface at 50 MHz, about 0.6 s. Frames also define what can be rewritten independently, which is the basis of partial reconfiguration and of readback for scrubbing radiation-induced upsets.

## Encoding multiplexer selects

Routing in modern FPGAs is built from multiplexers. A mux with $m$ inputs can store its select one-hot, one bit per input, or binary-encoded in $\lceil \log_2 m \rceil$ bits with a decoder. With 2050 muxes of 33 inputs, one-hot needs $2050 \times 33 = 67{,}650$ bits and encoded storage $2050 \times 6 = 12{,}300$. Fewer bits mean a smaller configuration memory and a shorter bitstream, while one-hot drives pass transistors directly with no decoder delay or area; real devices use mixtures, such as two-level muxes with one-hot selection at each level. The encoding is invisible to the router but defines how the bitstream writer translates a routed switch into bits, which is exactly what a bitstream database records.

## Going deeper

Kuon, Tessier and Rose (2008), sections on configuration; Lemieux and Lewis (2004) on multiplexer-based routing; the Project X-Ray documentation on frames and configuration.

label: Partial reconfiguration
lesson:
# Partial reconfiguration

Partial reconfiguration rewrites the configuration of one region while the rest of the device keeps running. A static region holds the interfaces; reconfigurable regions swap between modules. The flow must floorplan regions on frame boundaries, freeze or decouple their interfaces during a swap, and generate partial bitstreams, and the size of those bitstreams sets how fast the device can switch functions.

## Partial bitstream size

Because frames are the unit of configuration, a reconfigurable region is aligned to frame boundaries, typically whole columns within a clock region. The partial bitstream contains every frame of the region: if the region spans $c$ columns over $r$ rows, each column-row needs $F$ frames, and a frame has $w$ 32-bit words, the payload is $c \cdot r \cdot F \cdot w \cdot 4$ bytes. With $c = 5$, $r = 2$, $F = 28$ and $w = 101$, that is 113,120 bytes, about 110.5 KB. The partial bitstream scales with the region, not with the device, which is the point: a small region swaps quickly. Headers and commands add a little; frames that hold hard blocks or memory contents can add much more.

## Reconfiguration time

An internal configuration port lets the design itself load a partial bitstream, typically one 32-bit word per cycle. At 125 MHz the port moves $4 \times 125 \times 10^6 = 500$ MB/s, so a 428,544-byte partial bitstream takes $428{,}544 / 500 = 857.1$ microseconds. Real throughput can be lower when the bitstream is fetched from external memory or when the port runs below its maximum clock. During the swap, the region's outputs are undefined, so the static region must decouple them, holding handshakes idle or isolating the interface, and must reset the new module once it is loaded. These are the steps that vendor flows such as AMD's dynamic function exchange automate around the bitstream itself.

## When it pays

Partial reconfiguration time-multiplexes hardware. If each swap costs $t_r$ and the loaded accelerator then runs for $t_t$, the region computes for a fraction $t_t / (t_t + t_r)$ of the time. With $t_r = 8.5$ ms and $t_t = 30$ ms, that is 77.9%; with $t_t = 1$ ms it would be 10.5%. Swapping pays when tasks run long compared with reconfiguration, or when the alternative is a larger, more expensive device. It costs floorplanning freedom: the region's resources are reserved, the static logic cannot use them, and the placer and router must keep static nets out of the region except for its declared partition pins. Every module must fit the region's resource mix, so regions are sized for the largest module.

## Going deeper

Vipin and Fahmy, "FPGA Dynamic and Partial Reconfiguration: A Survey of Architectures, Methods, and Applications", ACM Computing Surveys (2018); AMD's Vivado user guide on dynamic function exchange (UG909).

label: The open FPGA toolchain
lesson:
# The open FPGA toolchain

An open FPGA toolchain is a complete, source-available flow from Verilog to bitstream: Yosys for synthesis, nextpnr or VPR for packing, placement and routing, and a documented bitstream database with its packing tool. It is what lets a tool designer read, change and measure every stage, and it is the platform for most FPGA CAD research and for agent experiments on real devices.

## The stages and their files

For iCE40 the flow is Yosys with synth_ice40, writing a JSON netlist; nextpnr-ice40, reading the JSON netlist, a pin constraint file and the device database, and writing a textual configuration; and icepack, turning that into the binary bitstream. ECP5 is the same with synth_ecp5, nextpnr-ecp5 and ecppack over the Project Trellis database. The VTR flow is the research counterpart: a Verilog front end, ABC for LUT mapping, and VPR for packing, placement, routing and timing on an architecture written in XML. In VPR-based flows for real devices, the routed design is written as FASM, a list of enabled configuration features, which a database turns into frames.

## Real devices versus architecture models

nextpnr's architectures are real chips: the device database fixes every tile, wire and switch, and the output must load and run. VPR's architecture is a parameter: the XML file defines logic blocks, segment lengths, switch patterns and hard blocks, and VPR builds the routing-resource graph from it, so a researcher can evaluate an FPGA that has never been built. That is why VPR defaults to searching for the minimum channel width, an architecture metric, while nextpnr routes on the fixed fabric and reports timing from the device's delay data. Both share the same algorithms: annealing or analytical placement, and PathFinder-style negotiated routing. Choosing the tool means choosing between bit-exact devices and architectural freedom.

## Running fair experiments

Open flows make controlled experiments possible, but only if they are controlled. Placement is randomized, so a result needs several seeds, and a design near its limit can pass timing on one seed and fail on another. A change to one stage must hold every other stage fixed: the same benchmarks, architecture file, and downstream placer and router when evaluating a packer. A router change that lowers minimum channel width must also report critical-path delay and run time at a relaxed width, since routability can be bought with delay. And the bitstream database is itself data that can be wrong, so its coverage limits what an open flow can target. These are the habits that turn a toolchain into an instrument.

## Going deeper

Shah et al., "Yosys+nextpnr: An Open Source Framework from Verilog to Bitstream for Commercial FPGAs", FCCM (2019); Murray et al., "VTR 8", ACM TRETS (2020); the nextpnr and Yosys documentation.

lesson:
# Documenting bitstreams: IceStorm, Trellis, X-Ray

Vendors do not publish the bit-level format of their FPGAs. Projects such as IceStorm (Lattice iCE40), Trellis (Lattice ECP5) and X-Ray (AMD Xilinx 7-series) recovered it, producing databases that map every configurable feature to its bits. Those databases are what make open place and route and open bitstream generation possible, and they are a lesson in how to recover a hidden mapping.

## What a database records

A bitstream database lists, for every tile type, each configurable feature (a LUT's truth-table bits, a flip-flop's mode, a routing multiplexer's input, an I/O standard) and the configuration bits that enable it, as frame and bit offsets relative to the tile's base address. Tiles of the same type share one entry, and each tile instance records its base, which keeps the database compact. With it, a tool can write a bitstream for any design by setting the bits of the features the design uses, and can read a bitstream back by asking which features its bits enable. IceStorm covers iCE40, Trellis covers ECP5, and X-Ray covers 7-series parts such as Artix-7.

## Fuzzing

The mapping is found by fuzzing. Generate many small designs that differ in a controlled way, such as whether one routing switch is used, build each with the vendor tools, and compare the bitstreams. Bits that change exactly when the feature changes encode it. Vendor tools make side changes, so a single pair of designs is not enough: a toggle that flips eight bits, three of which also flip in unrelated runs, leaves five candidates, and more varied designs are needed to isolate the real ones. Fuzzers therefore build hundreds or thousands of designs per feature class and solve for the bits that are consistent across all of them. The process is statistical and incremental, and coverage grows feature class by feature class.

## Limits and uses

A database is only as good as its coverage and correctness. A wrong entry produces a bitstream that loads and misbehaves, so databases are validated against vendor-built bitstreams; rarely used tile features, such as unusual I/O modes, are where gaps tend to remain. Beyond place and route, a documented bitstream allows readback into a netlist (icebox_vlog does this for iCE40), which lets the configured hardware be compared with the intended design. For a new family with no database, the first part of an open flow that can be built is synthesis to the documented primitives; packing, placement, routing and bitstream generation all need the device database.

## Going deeper

The Project IceStorm, Project Trellis and Project X-Ray documentation; the F4PGA documentation for the VPR-based 7-series flow.

lesson:
# Vendor FPGA flows

Each FPGA vendor ships its own implementation suite: AMD Vivado (with Vitis for software and HLS), Intel Quartus Prime, Lattice Radiant (and Diamond for older families) and Microchip Libero SoC. They run the same stages as the open flows with signoff-grade timing data and full device and IP coverage. A tool designer should know their stages, constraint formats and artifacts, because they are the baselines open tools are measured against.

## Which tool for which device

Vivado implements AMD (Xilinx) 7-series, UltraScale and later devices; Vitis sits beside it for embedded software, HLS kernels and acceleration platforms, whose hardware is still implemented through Vivado. Quartus Prime handles Intel (Altera) families such as Cyclone and Stratix. Lattice Radiant targets Lattice's newer families, while Diamond covers older ones such as ECP5. Microchip Libero SoC handles PolarFire, SmartFusion2 and IGLOO2, with third-party synthesis built in. The tools differ in names and file formats but agree on the flow: synthesis, implementation (placement and routing), timing analysis and bitstream generation, driven by SDC-style constraints.

## Stages and constraints

In Vivado's non-project Tcl flow the steps after synthesis are opt_design, place_design, phys_opt_design, route_design and write_bitstream; constraints are XDC, which uses SDC syntax for clocks, I/O delays and timing exceptions. Quartus runs Analysis and Synthesis, then the Fitter (placement and routing), the Assembler (programming files) and the Timing Analyzer, with SDC constraints. Each step reads and writes an in-memory design database. Physical optimization after placement, such as replicating high-fanout drivers or retiming registers, uses placement information that synthesis did not have, which is a recurring pattern: later stages repair what earlier stages could only estimate.

## Checkpoints and comparisons

Vivado writes design checkpoints that store the netlist, constraints and physical state after each step, so an engineer can reopen a routed design and try a timing fix in minutes instead of rerunning hours of implementation. When comparing a vendor flow with an open one, the two use different heuristics and different timing data, so their reported $F_{max}$ values are not directly comparable; timing both routed results with one trusted timer separates algorithm from model. Vendor flows remain the choice for production designs because they cover every primitive and hard IP block with validated timing; open flows are the choice when the experiment changes the algorithm itself.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Seams and tiers in a placer and router

An agent-first FPGA placer or router is built in four layers: an immutable core that guarantees legality, strategy plug-ins for heuristics, parameters for tuning, and observation hooks for live state. Most customer requests then land as configuration or plug-ins, never as core edits. Deciding where each piece of VPR or nextpnr belongs is the design skill this concept practices.

## The four layers of a placer and a router

In a router, the core is the routing-resource graph's legality (a net uses only existing edges, and in the final solution no node exceeds its capacity) plus the wavefront kernel. Strategy is the cost function, the rip-up order and the net ordering. Parameters are base costs per segment type, $p_{fac}$ and its multiplier, $h_{fac}$, and the A* factor. Hooks are per-iteration callbacks exposing overuse and critical-path delay. In an annealing placer, the core is legalization and macro handling, such as carry chains moved as one; strategy is the move set and the cost terms; parameters are InnerNum, $\lambda$ and the criticality exponent; and hooks expose the cost and acceptance rate per temperature. The core is small and rarely touched.

## Placing a request in a change tier

A request goes to the smallest safe tier. Making one region's long wires 20% more expensive is Tier 1 when base costs per resource are already a parameter table. Penalizing routes that use more than two long wires in a row needs new logic, but if a CostProvider seam is called per node expansion with the partial path's context, it is a Tier 2 plug-in. A soft goal such as keeping two blocks within three columns belongs in a Tier 2 cost term, not in a Tier 3 edit to the legality check, which would turn a preference into a constraint and could make placements infeasible. For a router seam to serve both timing-driven and congestion-aware plug-ins, it must pass the node, its type and location, its occupancy, capacity and history, and the connection's criticality.

## Seams in hot loops

Router cost functions run millions of times per iteration, so a seam there must be cheap: plain data, no hidden state, no allocation, and deterministic for a given seed, so the hot kernel can still be compiled and inlined around it. After a Tier 2 plug-in lands, the differential test must show that only the targeted nets changed, that legality holds, and that QoR elsewhere is within seed noise. When every new placement objective has required editing the annealer's inner loop, the objective seam is missing; the fix is to move cost terms behind an interface so that such requests become plug-ins. Determinism is not optional, because golden and differential tests compare runs, and nondeterminism makes a regression indistinguishable from noise.

lesson:
# Agents tuning nextpnr and VPR options

Open FPGA tools expose dozens of options: placer effort, timing trade-off, router cost schedules, seeds. An agent can tune them with the harness loop, running experiments and promoting the best configuration. Because placement is randomized, the agent must treat results as samples, average over seeds and compare against noise, or it will promote lucky runs.

## Results are distributions

A placer seed changes the random moves and so the final placement; on a design near its limit, Fmax can vary by several percent across seeds. An agent evaluating one configuration therefore runs it on several seeds and logs the mean. With six seeds giving 131.5, 131.5, 134, 133.5, 131.5 and 126.5 MHz, the mean is 131.42 MHz. A single seed would conflate the effect of the configuration with the luck of the seed. The same is true of minimum channel width and run time. Logging every seed's result, not just the mean, also lets the agent see variance, which is itself a property of the configuration: a setting with a slightly lower mean and much smaller spread may be the better choice for production.

## Comparing configurations

The agent compares configurations by their means against a baseline run under the same seeds and benchmarks. With a baseline of 180, 171.5 and 176 MHz (mean 175.83) and three configurations averaging 167, 181.83 and 173.5 MHz, the best improves on the baseline by 6.00 MHz. The comparison is per design, on fixed tool versions and fixed constraints, and every run is logged so the experiment is reproducible. In the harness loop, a configuration change is Tier 1: no recompile, so an agent can run many experiments cheaply, in parallel, inside a sandbox with limits on CPU, memory and time. The expensive part is the runs, not the decisions.

## Gating promotion on noise

Before promoting a configuration, the agent requires its improvement to exceed the noise. A simple gate demands that the mean beat the baseline mean by more than the baseline's seed-to-seed range. With a baseline of 113.5, 115.5, 119 and 116.5 MHz (mean 116.13, range 5.5), candidates averaging 114, 118.5, 125.5 and 124.13 MHz, only the last two clear $116.13 + 5.5$. A statistical test on the seed samples is the principled version. Without such a gate, an agent that tries many configurations will eventually find one that looks better by chance, which is the multiple-comparisons trap. The promoted configuration then goes through golden tests on held-out designs before entering the shared library.

## Going deeper

label: Learned policies inside open placers
lesson:
# Learned policies inside open placers

Learned components are entering open FPGA placers: policies that choose which move to try in an annealer, models that predict routing congestion from a placement, and learned delay estimators. Used well, they speed up search inside an engine whose core still guarantees legality; used badly, they optimize a proxy and miss the real objective. The design question is where the learned piece sits and what grounds its reward.

## Learned policies behind seams

A move-selection policy decides which move type to propose next (a random swap, a move toward the median of a block's nets, a swap within a small window). The placer's core still checks legality, evaluates the exact cost change and applies the Metropolis rule, so a bad policy wastes moves but cannot corrupt the placement. This makes FPGA placement a good setting for tool-grounded reinforcement learning: the placer computes exact incremental costs in microseconds, giving a dense reward, namely the cost reduction each proposed move produced. A congestion predictor consulted by an analytical placer's cost function sits behind a similar seam. In both cases the learned piece is strategy, and legality and the real routing stay in their engines.

## Proxies and reward hacking

A reward based on bounding-box cost alone can teach a policy to make placements whose wirelength improves while routed timing gets worse, because routed delay was never in the reward. That is reward hacking on a proxy. The remedies are to include the real objective, to check samples periodically with the accurate engines, and to treat placement-stage estimates as fast proxies that need correction. Generalization is the other risk: a policy trained on small benchmarks must be shown to match or beat the default policy at equal run time on held-out designs of the target size. A policy that sometimes yields an unroutable result must pass the same routability and timing checks as any placer, with a fallback to the default when it fails.

## Judging and deploying learned placers

A claim that a learned placer beats VPR is meaningful only with the same architecture, benchmarks, routed timing and run-time budget for both. A learned move-type policy is easier to deploy than an end-to-end learned placer, because it plugs into an existing seam and inherits the engine's guarantees, so its failure modes are bounded. Replacing the annealer's acceptance test with a learned classifier, by contrast, changes the algorithm's convergence behavior and is a core change needing human review and full regression. When a policy is trained on a customer's designs on site, what returns to the shared library is the validated policy or its know-how, not the designs: the IP boundary is part of the architecture.

## Going deeper

Murray et al., "VTR 8", ACM TRETS (2020), for VPR's placement options.

label: Bitstream-level verification as the golden check
lesson:
# Bitstream-level verification as the golden check

On an FPGA, the bitstream is what the hardware actually runs, so it is the most authoritative artifact for checking a flow. Decoding a bitstream through its database and comparing the result with the intended design is the golden check for any change an agent makes to packing, placement, routing or bitstream generation. Knowing which check fits which change keeps agent experiments both fast and safe.

## Why the bits are the ground truth

Every earlier representation, the netlist, the placement, the routed database, is a tool's belief about the hardware. Errors in the bitstream writer or in the feature-to-bit database leave those beliefs intact while the bits are wrong, so simulation of the post-route netlist can pass while the device fails. With a documented database, open flows can decode a bitstream into a netlist of configured primitives and run equivalence checking against the synthesized design. A golden test for an engine change fixes benchmark designs, seeds and architecture, with known-good results that the new build must reproduce or match within tolerance, and a FASM or bitstream diff shows exactly which features changed.

## Matching the check to the change

Different changes need different contracts. A refactor of the bitstream writer that should change nothing is tested by byte-for-byte identity of bitstreams for a fixed set of routed designs. A placer or router change legitimately changes the bits, so bit identity is the wrong test: the contract is functional equivalence of the decoded bitstream, no illegal or shorted routes, and QoR at least as good. A router change that improves the timing report is not accepted on that report alone, because better timing from a wrong route is worthless. A feature diff limited to routing-switch features, with LUT and flip-flop features identical, is direct evidence that a change touched only routing.

## Golden checks in an agent loop

Decoding and formally checking every result is slower than reading a timing report, so an agent uses fast checks to explore and the bitstream-level check to gate promotion, like the accurate engines in a fast and accurate loop. Configurations that change how packing or routing is done must pass it before promotion; changes that leave the bits identical, such as report verbosity, can be shown so directly. A mismatch confined to one tile type while the logic matches points first at the database for that tile. And a reward for an agent that edits the router must be gated on legality and equivalence; otherwise lowering minimum channel width by producing wrong routes is the cheapest way to score.

## Going deeper

The Project IceStorm documentation for icebox_vlog; the Yosys documentation for equivalence checking.

label: Fast versus accurate timing estimation
prereqs: Fast and accurate engines in a modeling loop
lesson:
# Fast versus accurate timing estimation

FPGA flows estimate timing at every stage: from LUT depth during mapping, from a distance-based delay model during placement, and exactly only after routing. An agent running a continuous loop uses the fast estimates to decide what to try and recurses to the accurate timer where the estimate cannot be trusted. Measuring the estimator's error and choosing the guard band are what make that loop safe.

## Measuring the estimator

Compare the fast estimate with post-route static timing on the same paths. The mean absolute error, $\frac{1}{n}\sum |\hat s_i - s_i|$, summarizes how far off the estimate is. With slack estimates and routed values of (190, 190), (-50, -130), (460, 400), (380, 390), (450, 370) and (330, 390) ps, the absolute errors sum to 290 ps, so the MAE is 48.3 ps. The sign of the error matters as much as its size: placement-stage models ignore congestion, so they tend to be optimistic, predicting more slack than routing delivers. Measuring the error per design class, and refreshing it as the tools change, is part of maintaining the fast engine.

## Guard bands decide when to recurse

An agent trusts the fast estimate only when its slack exceeds a guard band $g$ and sends every other path to the accurate timer. With $g = 60$ ps and estimates of 150, -90, -60, 330, -40, -150 and 190 ps, four paths fall below 60 and go to the accurate engine. A larger guard band sends more paths, costing run time, while a smaller one risks trusting wrong estimates. A principled choice ties $g$ to the measured error distribution, for example a high percentile of the optimistic error. Placement and routing tools already work this way: they recompute criticalities from an approximate model frequently and from exact timing occasionally.

## False passes are the dangerous error

Two kinds of error are not symmetric. A pessimistic error, where the estimate predicts a violation that routing does not show, costs only extra work. A false pass, with estimated slack of 0 or more but negative routed slack, lets a violation through. With estimates and routed values of (-30, 50), (150, 100), (370, 380), (-20, -80), (20, -50) and (220, 280) ps, only the fifth path is a false pass. An agent's fast-accurate loop must be designed around the false-pass rate, not the average error: it is acceptable for the estimator to be noisy if the guard band makes false passes rare, and every promoted result is still signed off by the accurate timer.

## Going deeper

Marquardt, Betz and Rose, FPGA (2000), for placement-stage delay estimation.
